course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

themes.title: Interactions of humans with the environment
themes.question: How did geography, crops, resources, or disease shape choices?

themes.title: Economic systems

themes.example: Mali drew revenue from commerce through its territory.

questions.prompt: Which of the following tools used by European navigators originated in China?
choices: The caravel
The astrolabe
The fluyt
The magnetic compass
questions.explanation: The compass came to Europe from China.
choiceExplanations: The caravel was a Portuguese ship design.
The astrolabe was refined by scholars in the Islamic world.
The fluyt was a Dutch cargo ship.
The compass came to Europe from China.
questions.distinguisher: The astrolabe is also borrowed, but it was refined in the Islamic world, not invented in China.

questions.prompt: The caravel was especially useful for exploration because it
choices: carried enough cannons to conquer coastal cities
could sail against the wind using square and lateen sails
could carry very large cargoes over long distances with only a small crew
used oars so it could move without any wind
questions.explanation: Its mix of sails let it explore coasts and return against prevailing winds.
choiceExplanations: Caravels were small exploring ships, not heavily armed warships.
Its mix of sails let it explore coasts and return against prevailing winds.
Large cargo with a small crew describes the fluyt.
Caravels relied on sails, not oars.
questions.distinguisher: Carrying large loads with a small crew describes the later Dutch fluyt.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why Vasco da Gama hired a local pilot in East Africa?
choices: The pilot knew the Atlantic wind loops that would carry the fleet back to Portugal
The pilot knew the monsoon routes across the Indian Ocean to India
Portuguese law required ships to hire African sailors
The pilot could translate between Portuguese and Chinese

choiceExplanations: The pilot's knowledge concerned the Indian Ocean.
Indian Ocean sailors had long used the monsoons, and the pilot guided da Gama to Calicut.
There was no such law.
Da Gama was bound for India, not China.

choices: the end of overland trade across Eurasia
the discovery of the monsoon winds by Dutch sailors
higher shipping costs that limited Dutch trade
lower shipping costs that helped the Dutch dominate European trade
questions.explanation: Carrying large cargoes with small crews made Dutch shipping cheaper and more competitive.
choiceExplanations: Overland trade continued.
The monsoons had been known for centuries.
The fluyt lowered costs.
Carrying large cargoes with small crews made Dutch shipping cheaper and more competitive.

questions.prompt: Which of the following claims about navigation technology is most defensible?
choices: European voyages relied on tools and knowledge from across Afro-Eurasia
Navigation technology changed little between 1450 and 1750
European voyages relied mainly on tools and maps obtained from peoples of the Americas
Europeans invented every major navigational tool of the period
questions.explanation: This claim fits the evidence of borrowed tools combined with new ship designs.
choiceExplanations: This claim fits the evidence of borrowed tools combined with new ship designs.
New ships and wind knowledge changed navigation greatly.
The borrowed tools came from Asia and the Islamic world.
The compass, astrolabe, and lateen sail all came from outside western Europe.
questions.distinguisher: Borrowing is right, but the tools came from Afro-Eurasia, not the Americas.

questions.prompt: The volta do mar was a sailing technique that
choices: used the monsoons to cross the Pacific
used a wide loop into the Indian Ocean to reach the ports of southern China
used a wide loop into the Atlantic to catch winds back to Europe
allowed ships to sail straight north against the trade winds
questions.explanation: Captains swung far west to catch westerly winds home.
choiceExplanations: The monsoons blow in the Indian Ocean, not across the Pacific.
The technique was used in the Atlantic.
Captains swung far west to catch westerly winds home.
Sailing straight against the wind was what the loop avoided.
questions.distinguisher: A wide loop is right, but the volta do mar was an Atlantic technique for returning from Africa.

questions.prompt: The author's main argument in the first paragraph is that European navigation
choices: depended on tools developed in Asia and the Islamic world
was more advanced than navigation anywhere else in 1400
depended on tools invented by Portuguese shipbuilders
depended on tools developed in Asia and later lost by Europeans
questions.explanation: The compass, astrolabe, and lateen sail all came from outside Europe.
choiceExplanations: The compass, astrolabe, and lateen sail all came from outside Europe.
The passage stresses borrowing, not superiority.
The author says few tools were European inventions.
The passage says Europeans combined and used the tools.
questions.distinguisher: The borrowing is right, but nothing in the passage says the tools were lost; Europeans built on them.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 4.1 key concept: knowledge, scientific learning, and technology from the Classical, Islamic, and Asian worlds spread, enabling European maritime innovation
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing how historians explain European navigation technology, c. 1400–1600
stimulusBlocks.text:
Few of the tools European sailors used in the 1400s were European inventions. The magnetic compass came from China. The astrolabe, refined by scholars in the Islamic world, let navigators measure latitude by the height of the sun or stars. The triangular lateen sail, used for centuries by sailors in the Indian Ocean and Mediterranean, let ships sail closer to the wind.

Portuguese shipbuilders combined these elements in the caravel, a small, maneuverable ship with both square and lateen sails. Its design allowed sailors to explore the West African coast and return against the prevailing winds.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, the caravel's design made it possible to
choices: carry larger cargoes than any Asian ship
explore the African coast using only square sails, without any lateen sails
cross the Pacific without stopping
explore the West African coast and return against prevailing winds
questions.explanation: The mix of sails let caravels explore coasts and sail back against the wind.
choiceExplanations: Caravels were small ships.
Lateen sails were a key part of the design.
The passage concerns the African coast.
The mix of sails let caravels explore coasts and sail back against the wind.
questions.distinguisher: The caravel combined square and lateen sails; the lateen sail was what allowed sailing against the wind.

questions.prompt: The transfer of technology described in the passage is best understood in the context of
choices: earlier networks of exchange that connected the Americas and Asia
earlier networks of exchange that connected Afro-Eurasia
the Columbian Exchange after 1492
the Industrial Revolution in Britain
questions.explanation: Silk Roads, Indian Ocean, and Mediterranean trade had spread these tools before 1450.
choiceExplanations: The Americas were not linked to Asia before 1492.
Silk Roads, Indian Ocean, and Mediterranean trade had spread these tools before 1450.
The tools spread before 1492.
Industrialization came after 1750.
questions.distinguisher: Earlier networks are right, but before 1492 they linked Afro-Eurasia, not the Americas and Asia.

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, the volta do mar depended mainly on
choices: knowledge of monsoon winds gained from pilots who sailed the Indian Ocean
knowledge of Atlantic wind patterns gained over many voyages
new engines that allowed ships to sail into the wind
maps drawn by Chinese navigators
questions.explanation: Captains learned to use Atlantic winds by swinging west.
choiceExplanations: The passage connects pilots to the Indian Ocean, not the Atlantic loop.
Captains learned to use Atlantic winds by swinging west.
Ships had no engines in this period.
The passage does not mention Chinese maps.
questions.distinguisher: Monsoon knowledge mattered in the Indian Ocean; the volta do mar was an Atlantic technique.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 4.1 key concept: new tools, ship designs, and an improved understanding of regional wind and current patterns made transoceanic travel and trade possible
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing how sailors used Atlantic and Indian Ocean wind systems, c. 1450–1600
stimulusBlocks.text:
Sailing home from West Africa was harder than sailing out, because winds blew steadily from the north. Portuguese captains learned to swing far west into the open Atlantic, where westerly winds could carry them back to Europe. This long loop, sometimes called the volta do mar, depended on knowledge of wind patterns built up over many voyages.

In the Indian Ocean, European ships entered a world that already had detailed knowledge of the monsoon winds. When Vasco da Gama reached East Africa in 1498, he hired a local pilot to guide his fleet across the ocean to Calicut.

questions.prompt: The second paragraph would best support which of the following claims?
choices: European sailors discovered the monsoon winds on their first voyages
Indian Ocean trade began with Portuguese voyages
European sailors ignored local knowledge in Asia
European sailors relied on existing Indian Ocean knowledge
questions.explanation: Da Gama's hiring of a local pilot shows reliance on existing knowledge.
choiceExplanations: The monsoons were long known.
Indian Ocean trade was centuries old.
Da Gama relied on local knowledge.
Da Gama's hiring of a local pilot shows reliance on existing knowledge.
questions.distinguisher: Da Gama hired a pilot because the monsoon system was already known; Europeans did not discover it.
